title: Solar Water Heaters in Kenya: Heat-Pipe vs Flat-Plate, and What Size You Need
excerpt: How to size a solar water heater for your household, the difference between pressurized heat-pipe and flat-plate systems, installation tips and current prices.
seo_title: Solar Water Heaters in Kenya: Sizes, Types & Prices
seo_desc: How to choose a solar water heater in Kenya: 150L, 200L or 300L, heat-pipe vs flat-plate, pressurized systems, installation tips and current prices.
kw: solar water heater Kenya,solar water heater price Kenya
content:
Quick answer

As a starting point, allow about 40–50 litres of hot water per person per day: a 150L solar water heater suits 2–3 people, 200L suits 3–4 and 300L suits 5–6. Choose a pressurized heat-pipe (evacuated tube) system if you want strong performance on cooler or cloudy days or have hard water. A flat-plate system is a robust choice for sunny sites with good roof space. Pressurized systems in our shop cost from KSh 96,000 (150L) to KSh 184,000 (300L).

In this guide
  1. Why solar water heating pays off
  2. What size do you need?
  3. Heat-pipe vs flat-plate collectors
  4. Pressurized vs low-pressure systems
  5. Installation tips
  6. Prices in our shop
  7. FAQs

Heating water is one of the biggest electricity costs in many Kenyan homes, guest houses and rentals. Electric showers and instant heaters typically draw around 3,000W or more each while running. A solar water heater takes most of that load off your bill by heating water directly from the sun, without needing an inverter or batteries.

Why solar water heating pays off

  • It uses heat directly. A solar water heater captures the sun's heat, which is far more efficient than turning sunlight into electricity and then back into heat.
  • It protects your solar power system. Running electric showers from a battery system drains it quickly. Moving water heating to a solar water heater lets a smaller PV system cover the rest of the house (see our guide to sizing a solar system).
  • Hot water is stored. An insulated tank keeps water hot into the evening and next morning.

What size do you need?

Size the tank by the number of people and how they use hot water. A common starting point is 40–50 litres of hot water per person per day.

HouseholdSuggested tankOptions in our shop
2–3 people150LSeven Stars 150L heat-pipe
3–4 people200L200L heat-pipe or 200L flat-plate
5–6 people300L300L heat-pipe or 300L flat-plate

For guest houses, rentals and larger facilities, add up the hot water each unit uses, or ask us to size several systems together.

Heat-pipe vs flat-plate collectors

Pressurized heat-pipe (evacuated tube)

Each glass tube has a vacuum layer that insulates it, with a copper heat pipe inside that carries heat up to a manifold where it warms the water. Because the vacuum cuts heat loss, heat-pipe systems keep performing well in cooler, windy or partly cloudy weather. The water does not flow through the tubes themselves, which also makes them a good option where water is hard and causes scaling.

Direct flat-plate

A flat-plate collector is an insulated panel with a dark absorber plate and pipes behind glass. In a direct system the water passes through the collector itself. Flat-plate collectors are robust, have no glass tubes to break and suit sunny sites with good roof space. In very hard water areas, scaling inside a direct collector is something to plan for.

Heat-pipe (evacuated tube)Direct flat-plate
Cool or cloudy weatherPerforms very wellGood in strong sun
Hard waterBetter (water stays out of the tubes)Plan for scaling
RobustnessIndividual tubes can be replaced if brokenVery robust, no glass tubes
Price in our shop (200L)KSh 125,000KSh 131,000

Pressurized vs low-pressure systems

All the solar water heaters we currently stock are pressurized systems. A pressurized system delivers hot water at close to mains pressure, so showers and mixer taps work as they would with an electric heater. It needs a tank rated for pressure and safety valves, which come as part of a proper installation.

Low-pressure (gravity) systems are cheaper but rely on the tank's height for pressure, which often gives a weak shower flow.

Installation tips

  • Avoid shade. Mount the collector where it gets sun for most of the day, clear of water tanks, trees and taller buildings.
  • Keep a slight tilt. Kenya is close to the equator, so the sun is high for much of the year. A modest tilt lets rain wash dust off the collector.
  • Check the roof. A full 300L tank of water is heavy, so the roof structure must be able to carry it.
  • Plan for cloudy spells. Many installations include an electric backup element for long cloudy periods. Ask us whether the model you choose includes one.
  • Keep pipe runs short and insulated so hot water reaches the tap quickly and stays hot.

Prices in our shop

At the time of writing, pressurized solar water heaters in our shop are:

  • Seven Stars 150L heat-pipe: KSh 96,000
  • Seven SS Stars 200L heat-pipe: KSh 125,000
  • Seven Stars 200L flat-plate: KSh 131,000
  • Seven Stars 300L heat-pipe: KSh 168,000
  • Seven Stars 300L flat-plate: KSh 184,000

Check the product pages for current prices and availability. Installation depends on your roof and plumbing, and we quote it after seeing the site.

Tell us how many people live in the home and we'll recommend the right tank.

Get a recommendation

FAQs

Does a solar water heater work on cloudy days?

Yes, at reduced output. Heat-pipe collectors cope best with cloud and cool weather, and the insulated tank stores heat from sunnier hours. For long cloudy spells, an electric backup element keeps water hot.

Is a 200 litre solar water heater enough for a family of four?

For most families of four, yes. At 40–50 litres per person per day, four people need about 160–200 litres. If you take long showers or run a washing machine on hot water, consider 300L.

Do I need batteries or an inverter for a solar water heater?

No. A solar water heater heats water directly from the sun and stores it in an insulated tank, so it does not need batteries, panels or an inverter.

Heat-pipe or flat-plate for hard borehole water?

Heat-pipe systems are generally better with hard water because the water stays in the tank rather than flowing through the collector tubes, which reduces scaling in the collector.

title: Lithium vs Gel Batteries for Solar in Kenya: Usable Capacity, Lifespan and Real Cost
excerpt: A like-for-like comparison of lithium and gel solar batteries using real cycle ratings, warranties and prices, and when gel still makes sense.
seo_title: Lithium vs Gel Solar Batteries in Kenya: Which Is Cheaper?
seo_desc: Lithium vs gel solar batteries compared on usable capacity, cycle life, warranty and cost per kWh, using real Kenyan shop prices. Which should you buy?
kw: lithium vs gel battery Kenya,solar battery Kenya

img.name: lithium-solar-battery-cabinet-kenya.jpg
img.alt: Lithium solar battery cabinet installed by Solar Connect Kenya

content:
Quick answer

For most solar systems in Kenya, lithium (LiFePO4) batteries are the better long-term buy. They can be discharged far more deeply each day, need no maintenance and, on the manufacturers' own figures, last several times as many cycles as gel batteries. Gel batteries cost less up front for small systems, but you can only use about half their capacity. Compared on usable energy, the upfront cost is surprisingly close, and lithium delivers far more energy over its life.

In this guide
  1. Usable capacity
  2. Cycle life and lifespan
  3. Cost comparison using our shop prices
  4. Maintenance, weight and heat
  5. When gel still makes sense
  6. Choosing the right lithium battery
  7. FAQs

The battery is usually the most expensive part of a solar system after installation, and the one people most often regret choosing on price alone. Here is how lithium and gel batteries compare, using the specifications and prices of batteries we actually stock.

Usable capacity: the number that matters

A battery's label shows its total capacity, in amp-hours (Ah) at a voltage, or in kWh. How much of that you can use without damaging the battery depends on its chemistry:

  • The gel batteries in our shop list 50% depth of discharge. A 200Ah 12V gel battery holds 2.4 kWh, but you should only use about 1.2 kWh before recharging.
  • Our lithium batteries list much deeper discharge, with some Felicity models at 95% or more and Suness models rated at 90%. Planning around a conservative 80% still gives far more usable energy per kWh on the label.

This is why a "smaller" lithium battery often replaces a bank of larger gel batteries.

Cycle life and lifespan

A cycle is one discharge and recharge. In a solar home the battery cycles roughly once a day, so cycle life translates directly into years.

Battery in our shopListed cycle life
Felicity 100Ah and 150Ah gel batteries1,500 cycles at 50% depth of discharge
Felicity LPBF48150, LPBF48200, LPBF48300, LPBF48350 and FLA12100, FLA24100, FLA48100 lithiumover 6,000 cycles
SRNE SR-EOS10B, SVC 5.12kWh, Jinko JKS-B48100-HI6,000 cycles
Hinen B5000 Seriesup to 8,000 cycles
Suness EV-5.12M and EV-15.36Nover 8,000 cycles at 90% depth of discharge

Cycle figures are the manufacturers' listed ratings under test conditions. Real life depends on temperature, charging settings and how deeply the battery is discharged.

Warranties follow the same pattern. Our gel battery listings come with a 1-year warranty, while many of our lithium batteries list 3 to 5 years.

Cost comparison using our shop prices

Here is a like-for-like comparison for a 48V system using batteries we stock, at prices at the time of writing.

Gel optionLithium option
Battery4 x Felicity 200Ah 12V gel, wired to 48V1 x Felicity FLA48100 5.12 kWh 48V lithium
Total capacity9.6 kWh5.12 kWh
Usable per cycleabout 4.8 kWh (50%)about 4.1 kWh (planned at 80%)
Upfront price4 x KSh 29,600 = KSh 118,400KSh 115,000
Listed cycle life1,500 cycles (Felicity gel)over 6,000 cycles
Energy over listed lifeabout 7,200 kWhabout 24,600 kWh

For about the same upfront price and similar usable energy each night, the lithium battery is rated to deliver more than three times as much energy over its life, in one compact unit with no maintenance. Over the years that makes lithium the cheaper choice per kWh actually used.

Maintenance, weight and heat

  • Maintenance: both gel and lithium batteries are sealed. Gel batteries are maintenance-free in the sense that you never add water, but they need to be fully recharged regularly to avoid sulphation. Lithium batteries manage themselves through a built-in battery management system (BMS).
  • Weight and space: lithium packs are much lighter and smaller for the same usable energy, which helps with wall-mounted or indoor installations.
  • Heat: all batteries age faster in high temperatures. In hot areas such as the coast, install batteries in a shaded, ventilated space. Check each battery's listed operating temperature range.

When gel still makes sense

Gel batteries are still a reasonable choice when:

  • the system is small (lights, TV and phone charging) and the budget is tight,
  • you need a short-term or temporary backup, or
  • you are replacing a battery in an existing lead-acid or gel system whose charger settings cannot be changed for lithium.

Our gel range runs from KSh 15,500 (Felicity 100Ah 12V) to KSh 34,000 (R Energy 200Ah 12V).

Choosing the right lithium battery

  • Match the voltage to your inverter: 12V, 24V (25.6V) or 48V (51.2V).
  • Size by usable kWh for your night-time and outage needs. Our guide to sizing a solar system walks through the maths.
  • Check inverter compatibility. Many lithium batteries communicate with hybrid inverters over CAN or RS485, so confirm your inverter supports the battery brand.
  • Plan for expansion. Several models can be connected in parallel to add capacity later.

Popular 48V options in our shop include the Felicity 5kWh LPBF48100-M, the Hinen B5000 and the SRNE 10.24kWh SR-EOS10B for larger homes.

Upgrading from gel to lithium? We'll check your inverter is compatible first.

Check my setup

FAQs

Can I replace gel batteries with a lithium battery on my current inverter?

Often yes, but the inverter must support lithium charging settings, and ideally communicate with the battery. Tell us your inverter model and we will confirm before you buy.

Can I mix old and new batteries, or gel and lithium?

No. Mixing chemistries, ages or capacities in one bank causes uneven charging and shortens battery life. Replace the whole bank, or add identical lithium modules designed to run in parallel.

How many years does a lithium solar battery last?

At roughly one cycle a day, a battery listed for 6,000 cycles is rated for over 15 years of cycling under test conditions. Real-world life is shorter in heat or with poor charging settings. Warranties on our lithium batteries are typically 3 to 5 years.

What is LiFePO4?

Lithium iron phosphate, the lithium chemistry used in most home solar batteries. It is valued for its long cycle life and thermal stability.

title: Hybrid Inverter vs Inverter Charger: Which One Do You Need?
excerpt: What hybrid inverters and inverter chargers each do, high vs low frequency, single vs three phase, and how to choose the right one for your home or business.
seo_title: Hybrid Inverter vs Inverter Charger: Which Do You Need?
seo_desc: Hybrid inverter or inverter charger? How each works, high vs low frequency, prices in Kenya and which suits your home, business or backup needs.
kw: hybrid inverter vs inverter charger,hybrid inverter Kenya

img.name: hybrid-inverter-battery-installation-kenya.jpg
img.alt: Wall-mounted inverter and lithium battery installed in a Kenyan home

content:
Quick answer

A hybrid inverter combines an inverter, a solar (MPPT) charge controller and a battery charger in one unit. It runs your home on solar first, stores the extra in a battery and falls back to KPLC or a generator when needed. An inverter charger converts battery power to AC and recharges the battery from mains power, but to use solar panels you normally add a separate charge controller. Choose a hybrid inverter for a new solar system. An inverter charger suits backup-first setups, heavy motor loads, or adding panels to an existing system.

In this guide
  1. What a hybrid inverter does
  2. What an inverter charger does
  3. High frequency vs low frequency
  4. Side-by-side comparison
  5. Which one should you choose?
  6. Single phase, three phase and grid-tie
  7. FAQs

"Inverter" gets used for very different machines in Kenyan solar shops, and buying the wrong type is one of the most common reasons a system underperforms. This guide explains the two types we are asked about most, how they differ, and which suits your home or business.

What a hybrid inverter does

A hybrid inverter is the "brain" of a modern solar system. In a single box it:

  • converts DC power from your battery and panels into 240V AC for your sockets,
  • contains an MPPT solar charge controller, so panels connect straight to it,
  • charges the battery from solar, mains or a generator, and
  • switches between sources automatically, using solar first and the grid as backup.

Because everything is in one unit, installation is neater and the system can be set to make the most of free solar energy. Many larger models, such as the Deye 8kW single phase hybrid inverter, also offer app monitoring and support lithium batteries over a communication cable.

In our shop, hybrid inverters range from about KSh 25,000 for a 1kVA 12V unit to KSh 780,000 for a 50kW three phase commercial inverter, across Deye, Felicity Solar, Hinen, Solis, SRNE and GoodWe.

What an inverter charger does

An inverter charger is built mainly for backup. It converts battery power to AC during an outage, and when mains power returns it passes power through to your home and recharges the battery.

Most inverter chargers in our range do not include a solar charge controller. To add panels, you pair them with a separate MPPT charge controller that charges the battery from solar. MPPT controllers in our shop cost about KSh 11,500 to KSh 36,000, from 30A to 120A. Always check the product specifications, because features vary by model.

Inverter chargers in our shop, from Felicity Solar and Must, range from KSh 15,000 for a 0.7kVA unit to KSh 125,000 for a 10kVA 48V unit.

High frequency vs low frequency

You will also see inverters described as high frequency or low frequency. This describes how they are built inside:

  • Low-frequency inverters use a large transformer. They are heavier but very robust, and handle the start-up surge of motors, pumps and compressors well. Most of our inverter chargers, such as the Must EP3000 Plus and the Felicity IVPS range, are low frequency.
  • High-frequency inverters use electronic switching instead of a large transformer. They are lighter, more compact and usually cheaper for the same rating, and most hybrid inverters are built this way, for example the Felicity IVEM range.

For homes with pumps, welding equipment or large compressors, a low-frequency unit, or a high-frequency unit sized with generous headroom, avoids nuisance trips.

Side-by-side comparison

Hybrid inverterInverter charger
Main jobRun the home on solar, battery and grid togetherBackup power from batteries during outages
Solar panelsConnect directly (built-in MPPT)Usually need a separate charge controller
Charges battery fromSolar, mains or generatorMains or generator (solar via controller)
Typical buildMostly high frequencyOften low frequency
Motor and surge loadsGood, with headroomVery good (low-frequency models)
Best forNew solar installationsBackup-first setups and adding solar later
Price range in our shopKSh 25,000 – 780,000KSh 15,000 – 125,000

Which one should you choose?

Choose a hybrid inverter if:

  • you are installing solar panels now and want to cut your KPLC bill,
  • you want a tidy installation with one main unit and app monitoring, or
  • you are using lithium batteries and want them to communicate with the inverter.

Choose an inverter charger if:

  • your main goal is backup during outages and you may add panels later,
  • you run motor-heavy loads and want the surge tolerance of a low-frequency unit, or
  • you already have panels and a charge controller and need to replace the inverter.

Not sure what size you need? Start with our step-by-step guide to sizing a solar system for your home.

Single phase, three phase and grid-tie

Most Kenyan homes have a single phase supply, and single phase inverters suit them. Larger homes, flats, schools and commercial buildings often have a three phase supply. For these we supply three phase hybrid inverters such as the Deye SUN-10K-SG04LP3 and the Solis 15kW three phase model.

A third type, the grid-tie inverter (for example the SMA Sunny Tripower 6000TL), feeds solar power into your building alongside the grid with no battery. It lowers your daytime bill, but on its own it does not provide power during an outage.

Tell us what you want to power and we'll recommend the right inverter.

Ask on WhatsApp

FAQs

Can a hybrid inverter work without a battery?

Some hybrid inverters can run on solar and grid power without a battery, but you lose backup during outages. Whether it is supported depends on the model, so check the specifications or ask us before you buy.

Can I add solar panels to my existing inverter?

Usually yes. If you have an inverter charger, add an MPPT charge controller matched to your battery voltage and panels. If your inverter is already a hybrid, connect panels within its PV input limits.

What does kVA mean on an inverter?

kVA is the inverter's apparent power rating. The real power it can deliver in watts is usually a little lower. For example, our Felicity 2.5kVA inverter charger is rated at 2kW.

Is a more expensive inverter always better?

Not necessarily. The right inverter matches your load, battery voltage and supply type. An oversized or wrong-type inverter costs more and can run less efficiently.

title: How to Size a Solar System for Your Home in Kenya (Step by Step)
excerpt: Work out your daily energy use, then size the inverter, battery, panels and system voltage, with a worked example for a typical Kenyan family home and what it costs.
seo_title: How to Size a Solar System in Kenya: Step-by-Step Guide
seo_desc: Size a home solar system in Kenya in five steps: daily energy, inverter, battery, panels and voltage. Includes a worked example with real prices.
kw: solar system sizing Kenya,how to size a solar system

img.name: rooftop-solar-array-kenya.jpg
img.alt: Rooftop solar array installed by Solar Connect Kenya

content:
Quick answer

To size a home solar system in Kenya, add up how many watt-hours your appliances use in a day, then size four things from that number: the inverter (from the appliances that run at the same time), the battery (from the energy you need at night and during outages), the solar panels (daily energy ÷ sun hours, with a margin for losses) and the system voltage (12V, 24V or 48V). A typical family home using about 2.7 kWh a day is well served by a 3kVA 24V hybrid inverter, about 2.5–5 kWh of lithium battery and roughly 1.2 kW of panels.

In this guide
  1. List your appliances and daily energy
  2. Size the inverter
  3. Size the battery
  4. Size the solar panels
  5. Choose the system voltage
  6. Worked example and what it costs
  7. Common sizing mistakes
  8. FAQs

Most solar problems we are called to fix in Nairobi and on the coast are sizing problems, not equipment problems: an inverter that trips when the fridge starts, a battery that is flat by midnight, or panels that never fully recharge the battery. Getting the numbers right before you buy avoids all three. Here is the same method our team uses, step by step.

Step 1: List your appliances and work out daily energy

Write down every appliance you want solar to power, its power in watts (on the label or in the manual) and how many hours a day it runs. Multiply watts by hours to get watt-hours (Wh), then add them up.

AppliancePowerHours a dayEnergy a day
8 LED bulbs10W each5400 Wh
TV and decoder100W5500 Wh
Wi-Fi router15W24360 Wh
Fridgesee energy labelcycles on and offabout 1,200 Wh
Phones and a laptop60W4240 Wh
Totalabout 2,700 Wh (2.7 kWh)

These are example figures. A fridge's compressor switches on and off, so use the yearly kWh on its energy label divided by 365 rather than its rated watts × 24.

Leave out heavy heating loads such as electric showers, kettles, irons and cookers unless you are planning a large system. They draw 1,500–3,000W each and are far cheaper to run on gas or a solar water heater.

Step 2: Size the inverter from what runs at the same time

The inverter has to supply every appliance that is switched on at once, plus the brief start-up surge of anything with a motor or compressor (fridges, freezers, pumps), which can draw several times its running power for a moment.

  • Add up the watts of everything that could run together. In our example that is lights, TV, router, fridge and laptop: roughly 400–500W.
  • Allow headroom for start-up surges and for appliances you will add later. Running an inverter close to its limit all the time shortens its life.
  • For this home, a 3kVA inverter is a comfortable fit.

For most new installations we recommend a hybrid inverter, because it combines the inverter, solar charge controller and battery charger in one unit. If you mainly need backup and plan to add panels later, an inverter charger can also work. Our guide on hybrid inverters vs inverter chargers explains the difference.

Step 3: Size the battery from your night-time and backup needs

Batteries carry you through the evening, overnight and any power cuts. Work out the energy you use when the sun is down (in the example, about 1.5–1.6 kWh for lights, TV, router and the fridge overnight) and how long you want backup to last during an outage.

Then size by usable capacity, not the number on the label:

  • Lithium (LiFePO4) batteries can be discharged deeply every day. Many in our range list 80–95% depth of discharge, so a 2.56 kWh battery gives you roughly 2 kWh of usable energy.
  • Gel batteries should only be discharged to about half. The gel batteries in our shop list 1,500 cycles at 50% depth of discharge, so a 200Ah 12V gel battery (2.4 kWh) gives about 1.2 kWh of usable energy per cycle.

For our example home, a 2.56 kWh 24V lithium battery covers a normal night. A 5 kWh battery adds a comfortable buffer for long outages and future appliances. See lithium vs gel batteries for a full cost comparison.

Step 4: Size the solar panels from daily energy and sun hours

Most of Kenya receives roughly 4 to 6 kWh of solar energy per square metre per day, depending on location and season. For sizing, we treat that as about 5 peak sun hours and allow around 25% for real-world losses (heat, dust, wiring, battery charging).

Panel watts ≈ daily energy ÷ (sun hours × 0.75)

For the example: 2,700 Wh ÷ (5 × 0.75) ≈ 720W. We then round up so the panels can run the house during the day and recharge the battery, which gives about 1.2 kW. That is two modern panels such as the Jinko 580W monocrystalline panel.

Shade matters more than most people expect. A tree or water tank shading part of the array for a few hours can cut output noticeably, so we check the roof before finalising the design.

Step 5: Choose the system voltage

Battery-based systems run at 12V, 24V or 48V. Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, so thinner cables, less heat and better efficiency. As a rule of thumb:

System sizeTypical voltageSuits
Up to about 1.5kVA12VLights, TV, phones, a small fridge
About 3kVA24VA family home with a fridge and electronics
5kVA and above48VLarger homes, borehole pumps, offices and shops

The inverter, battery and charge controller must all match the chosen voltage.

Worked example and what it costs

Putting the example together: about 2.7 kWh a day, a 3kVA 24V hybrid inverter, 2.5–5 kWh of 24V lithium battery and about 1.2 kW of panels, plus breakers, surge protection, cabling, mounting and earthing.

That is close to our 3kW 24V hybrid solar system package: 4 x 550W panels, a 3.3kW 24V hybrid inverter and a 5kWh Felicity lithium battery, with accessories, transport and installation included, listed at KSh 300,000. Our other complete solar packages range from a 1.5kVA 12V system at KSh 160,000 to a 10kW 48V system at KSh 565,000.

If you prefer to buy components, typical prices in our shop at the time of writing are a 3kVA 24V hybrid inverter from KSh 34,000, a 2.56 kWh 24V lithium battery at KSh 80,000 and 580W panels at KSh 10,440 each. Prices change, so check the product pages for current figures.

Common sizing mistakes

  • Sizing the battery by its label. A 200Ah gel battery does not give you 200Ah of usable energy.
  • Forgetting start-up surges. Fridges and pumps can trip an inverter that looks big enough on paper.
  • Too few panels. The array has to power the day's loads and refill the battery. Otherwise the battery slowly runs down day after day.
  • Mixing voltages or brands without checking compatibility. Lithium batteries in particular need the right inverter settings or communication cable.
  • Putting heating loads on solar. Electric showers and kettles are the fastest way to drain a battery.

Send us your appliance list and we'll check the numbers for free.

Get my system sized

FAQs

How many solar panels do I need for a 3kVA inverter?

It depends on your daily energy use, not just the inverter size. For a typical home using 2.5–3 kWh a day, about 1.2 kW of panels (two 580W panels) is a good starting point. Heavier daytime use or a bigger battery needs more panels.

How long will a 5 kWh lithium battery last during a blackout?

Divide usable energy by your load. At 80% depth of discharge a 5 kWh battery gives about 4 kWh. Running lights, TV, Wi-Fi and a fridge (roughly 300W on average) that is around 13 hours; with only lights and Wi-Fi it is much longer.

Can solar run a fridge and a borehole pump?

Yes, if the inverter can handle the start-up surge and the panels and battery cover the extra energy. Pumps are best run during the day straight from solar. They usually push a home towards a 5kVA 48V system.

Should I choose 24V or 48V?

Around 3kVA, 24V is common and cost-effective. From 5kVA upwards, or if you expect to expand, 48V is more efficient and gives you more inverter and battery options.
